sut.config_delta:
The 16 GiB shape of kfk-exclusive, re-established on 2026-09-07 and judged healthy before the series, with one variable added: agent reachability.

OpenNMS Core
  VM: 8 vCPU, 16 GiB; opennms.conf JAVA_HEAP_SIZE 10240, JAVA_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE 8192
  collectd-configuration.xml: threads 250, thresholding-enabled false on every service
  snmp-config (Config Manager): timeout 1800 ms, retry 1, so a failing collection costs 3.6 s of thread time;
                                max-repetitions 5 for 10.42.0.0/16
  org.opennms.core.ipc.rpc.kafka.ttl: unset, 20,000 ms default; never reached
  G1, NativeMemoryTracking summary, 13 daemons disabled, Syslogd enabled, log4j2 instrumentation INFO
  org.opennms.features.kafka.producer.cfg: forward.metrics true, metricTopic metrics; no compression anywhere

Fleet: 11,000 nl6 devices, 11,004 collectable services, 10.42.0.0/16 octets 0-43, 144 interfaces each;
       netem delay 75ms 25ms on netsim enp6s19

The outages, all silent drops on netsim (bin/level.sh <on|off> <level>)
  25%: iptables -I FORWARD 1 -o veth-sim-host -d 10.42.0.0/21, 10.42.8.0/23, 10.42.10.0/24 -j DROP
       (octets 0-10, 2,750 devices)
  50%: 10.42.0.0/20, 10.42.16.0/22, 10.42.20.0/23 (octets 0-21, 5,500)
  75%: 10.42.0.0/19, 10.42.32.0/24 (octets 0-32, 8,250)
  100%: 10.42.0.0/18 (all 44 blocks, 11,000)

The pulse: 100% on 16:07:28Z, off 16:13:14Z (one cycle), run to clear the 4,404 alarms orphaned by the
           external restart of 15:33Z

Minion stock (2 GiB default heap). PostgreSQL pgtune profile with SSL.

The healthy baseline window is 11:00-11:15Z of the same day (record baseline-0 in levels.jsonl). An earlier full outage on this same deployment, for reference: the netsim FORWARD ACCEPT rule removed at 10:28:02Z and restored at 10:43:12Z.

workload.generator_scenario: nl6 cisco_crs_x.json, 11,000 devices, 144 interfaces each, SNMP v2c, 10.42.0.0/16 octets 0-43, netem delay 75ms 25ms on the simulator, GETBULK max-repetitions 5; 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of the fleet unreachable in turn

experiment.question: How does this deployment deal with SNMP agent outages: what does an unreachable agent cost, is the healthy remainder protected, what does recovery cost, and what does the max-repetitions=5 tuning have to do with any of it?
experiment.plan: One variable, the share of the fleet dropped silently, in whole /24 blocks of 250 devices: 11 blocks (25%), 22 (50%), 33 (75%), 44 (100%). Each level is applied on netsim's FORWARD chain ahead of the rule that carries SNMP into the simulator's namespace, held three collection cycles, judged over its second and third cycle by bin/judge.py, removed, and followed by two cycles of recovery before the next. Delivered work is read from the Core's metrics stream to Kafka against the healthy baseline, because the completion counter counts failed collections as completed. bin/monitor.py logs one line a minute including the events and alarms tables.

figures.title: CPU busy through the four levels: Core, Minion and database
figures.note: Levels on the FORWARD chain: 25% 13:50:47 to 14:06:10, 50% 14:22:45 to 14:38:23 (a first attempt 14:15:51 to 14:22:29 was cut short and discarded), 75% 14:48:13 to 15:04:17, 100% 15:14:11 to 15:30:25, each with two cycles of recovery after; then a one-cycle 100% pulse 16:07:28 to 16:13:14 to clear the alarms the external restart had orphaned, which doubles as the clean recovery from a total outage. Every machine steps down with the share of dead agents: a failed collection decodes, stores and looks up nothing. The 97% at 15:36 is the reload after an external restart of OpenNMS at 15:33.

figures.title: Collectd thread pool occupancy through the four levels, against its 250-thread ceiling
figures.note: Levels on the FORWARD chain: 25% 13:50:47 to 14:06:10, 50% 14:22:45 to 14:38:23 (a first attempt 14:15:51 to 14:22:29 was cut short and discarded), 75% 14:48:13 to 15:04:17, 100% 15:14:11 to 15:30:25, each with two cycles of recovery after; then a one-cycle 100% pulse 16:07:28 to 16:13:14 to clear the alarms the external restart had orphaned, which doubles as the clean recovery from a total outage. A dead agent holds a thread for one timeout and one retry, 3.6 s, against 5.2 s for a live one by Little's law on this run, so occupancy falls with every level. The pool pegged at 250 from 15:35 is that restart's scheduling wave.

figures.title: Thread time per collection through the four levels, against the 3.6 s an unreachable agent costs

source.panel: derived: Collectd active threads / collections per second

figures.note: Little's law read backwards: busy threads over collections per second is the mean time a collection holds a thread. It is derived from the same two captures as the threads and throughput figures, not a metric the Core exports, and both terms are smoothed over 5 minutes, one full collection interval, because the schedule swings both of them by more than the effect within a cycle. Scoped to the four levels, 13:45 to 15:32 UTC, and so narrower than every other figure here: after the 15:33 restart the completion rate briefly falls to near zero and the ratio is undefined. The floor is configuration, not tuning: an unreachable agent costs one 1,800 ms timeout and one retry, 3.6 s, whatever max-repetitions is set to. The recovery gaps between levels are two cycles long and the smoothing bleeds across their edges, so the curve peaks near 5 s there rather than at the baseline's 5.18 s.

answers.question: What does an unreachable SNMP agent cost the Core, the Minion and the database?
Is the healthy remainder still collected on time while a quarter, a half, three quarters of the agents are down?
What does the max-repetitions=5 tuning have to do with how outages land?
What does each outage cost the event path, and what does recovery cost?
What does a clean recovery from a total agent outage look like on this deployment?
What should an operator watch for, and is a 250-thread pool the right size for this fleet?
Which agent outages are not this one?

gaps.question: Is an unreachable agent the right partial outage?
gaps.why: Every dead agent fails on its first PDU after one timeout and one retry, so it is the cheapest failure the collector has. The expensive one is the agent that answers late or answers some tables and not others, which may hold a thread through as many as 61 timeouts. That outage was not run, and the gap below on Collectd's timeout semantics has to be closed before its cost can even be stated.

gaps.question: Does Collectd abandon a collection at the first timeout, or continue to the next table?
gaps.why: Not established in this series. A dead agent returns after one timeout and one retry, 3.6 s, which is consistent with either semantics because there is nothing left to ask. The degraded-agent budgets in the tuning section assume it continues and so eats a timeout per unanswered PDU; if it abandons the collection at the first timeout, a degraded agent costs the same 3.6 s a dead one does and those budgets do not apply.

gaps.question: Was max-repetitions varied in this run?
gaps.why: No. Every level ran at max-repetitions=5. The 61-against-149 PDU counts and the max-repetitions=2 thread times quoted in the tuning section come from two earlier searches on this same Core class, 8 vCPU with a 10 GiB heap, the same simulated device and the same netem, at a different fleet size and pool: pm-snmp-agent-latency-mr5 and pm-snmp-sizing-rule. The degraded-agent numbers derived from them are arithmetic on this deployment's timeout and interval, not measurements.

gaps.question: Are the levels comparable to each other?
gaps.why: They were run in ascending order with two recovery cycles between them, each judged over its own second and third cycle; the 100% level repeats the earlier full-outage test on the same deployment.

gaps.question: Does max-repetitions=5 still help when the agent is slow through its own load?
gaps.why: netem makes every agent slow per packet, uniformly, and against that failure mode fewer requests is strictly fewer timeouts. An agent slow because its own processor is loaded may fail a five-repetition GETBULK it would have answered at two, in which case the attribute moves the wrong way. Nothing in this lab can produce that failure mode or distinguish the two.

gaps.question: Does the 16 GiB Core at 11,000 devices stand for a Core at its knee?
gaps.why: This fleet leaves 40% of the Core's CPU and a quarter of its pool spare; every level here makes the Core lighter. The recovery burst of a level, one success event and one alarm clear per device, is the part a Core at 96% would feel.

gaps.question: Is the Core's transmit to Kafka a fair measure of delivered work?
gaps.why: The Core's link to Kafka carries the metrics topic and the RPC requests; the requests are small and their share does not change with the level, and the RPC responses it receives are not in the transmit direction. Delivered share is that transmit against the healthy baseline, and it lands within 3 points of the expected share at every level; it is a proxy, not a count of samples.

gaps.question: One window per level?
gaps.why: Each level is one ten-minute window over two cycles, once. The steps are large, a quarter of the fleet each, and the response is linear in the dead share, so the shape is not in doubt; the per-level constants are single samples.

gaps.question: Is an orphaned alarm after a mid-recovery restart expected behaviour?
gaps.why: The collector that came up after the 15:33Z restart had no record of which services were failed and raised no success event for the 4,404 still down, leaving their major alarms open with nothing to clear them. Whether alarmd or collectd is expected to reconcile collector state against the open alarm table on startup was not investigated, and no issue has been filed.
